extracted.intended_audience: scientists, researchers, and philosophers of science concerned with induction, experimental design, and assessing empirical generalizations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether observed regularities are empirical (derivative) laws or genuine laws of causation, and for determining when coincidences exceed what chance would produce. Includes signs of derivation, methods to eliminate chance, and when to invoke probability theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws limited to observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws (derivative laws unresolved into their elements) can only be received as true within the limits of time, place, and circumstance in which they have been found true by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extend empirical generalizations beyond the specific temporal, spatial, and circumstantial limits of observation without further evidence (experiment or deductive explanation). Example/anti-pattern: inferring terrestrial stratigraphic ordering applies to the moon or other planets despite unknown original planetary collocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement yields only empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: When a generalization rests solely on the Method of Agreement, it never proves causes and therefore only establishes empirical (derivative) laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat results obtained by simple observation (Method of Agreement) as empirical until confirmed by the Method of Difference or explained a priori. Avoid claiming causal laws from agreement-only inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to confirm by Method of Difference or deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: An observed uniformity must be either confirmed by the Method of Difference (experimental contrast) or explained deductively (a priori) to be elevated from an empirical law to a law of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer reviewers should require experimental contrasts or theoretical accounts that trace derivation into ultimate laws before accepting claims of causal generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of authority of empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws vary in authority according to reason to presume they are resolvable into laws alone or into laws plus collocations; some empirical laws are more likely to be derivative of simpler causal laws than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how plausible it is that a uniformity arises from common simpler causes versus accidental collocation; sequences in organismal development are more likely resolvable into common causes than sequences in geological superposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign 1 — evidence of intermediate link(s) implies derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is evidence of some intermediate phenomenon (an intermediate link x) between antecedent a and consequent b, then the law 'a causes b' is likely derivative (resolvable into a causes x and x causes b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for plausible unobserved intermediate processes (e.g., corpuscular interactions in chemistry or physiology). Their suspected existence weakens claims that an observed antecedent is an ultimate cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign 2 — complex antecedent suggests compound causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the antecedent is an extremely complex phenomenon, its effects are probably in part the compound effects of its different elements, implying the observed law is derivative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an antecedent comprises heterogeneous parts whose separate laws could combine to produce the observed effect (examples: weight as sum of particles; meteorological barometer changes as mixture of air and vapor). Simpler ultimate laws are more probable; complexity argues for further decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of causes undermines simple agreement-based inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a phenomenon may have many possible causes, two or more cases sharing only one common antecedent A do not prove a causal relation between A and the phenomenon a; plurality of causes is a characteristic imperfection of the Method of Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require multiplicity of diverse instances and consider alternative causal elements; use additional methods to reduce uncertainty from multiple possible causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of chance as lack of grounds for uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance is best understood as a coincidence from which we have no ground to infer a uniformity: two or more phenomena conjoined without reason to infer repeatable connection (i.e., not causally related nor effects of the same lawful collocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing apparent regularities, distinguish between true causal connection and mere casual conjunctions of independent causes; recurrence alone does not eliminate the possibility of casual coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence is not proof of law — compare to chance expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere recurrence or frequent recurrence of a coincidence does not prove it is due to a law; one must ask whether it occurs more often than chance (i.e., more often than would be expected if the phenomena were independent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate observed frequency relative to the frequency expected under independence (base rates). High absolute coincidence may still be expected by chance if one phenomenon is nearly always present (fixed stars example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for base rates when assessing coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidential weight of coincidences depends on the individual frequencies of the phenomena (their base rates); e.g., if A is very common, A will co-occur with B often even if unrelated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtract the expected coincidences due to ordinary frequencies of A and B to obtain the residual evidence for a causal connection. Peer reviewers should check whether authors have adjusted for base rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of expected coincidence from independent frequencies
rubrics_metrics.description: If A occurs in p proportion of cases and B in q proportion, then under independence their expected joint occurrence is p*q; any observed excess (or deficit) beyond this expectation indicates connection (or repugnance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the product rule for independent probabilities to estimate expected coincidence (example: A in 1/2, B in 1/3 -> expected co-occurrence 1/6). Compare observed co-occurrence to this baseline to infer linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residual analysis (excess or deficit) indicates connection or repugnance
rubrics_metrics.description: If A occurs more frequently among cases with B than without B (and vice versa), there is some causal connection; if less frequently, there is repugnance or counteracting causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess conditional proportions (P(A|B) vs P(A|not B)). The residual beyond chance is the evidence for a law. Reviewers should demand this conditioned-frequency analysis when causal claims are made from observational data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes — constant cause plus variable causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a constant cause A is habitually blended with many variable causes, the observed effect is the sum of A's effect and variable (chance) effects; one must estimate A's effect by repeated trials preserving A and averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design repeated trials keeping A constant and vary background conditions; compute the mean over many trials. If different sets of sufficiently numerous experiments yield the same mean, that mean estimates the effect of A. This is 'Elimination of Chance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of Chance via repeated trials and mean stabilization
rubrics_metrics.description: To eliminate the effect of numerous floating unassignable causes, make many trials preserving the suspected constant cause and use the average (mean) of results; the test of sufficiency is when further trials do not materially change the mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the number and variety of trials are sufficient so the sample mean has stabilized within the accuracy required. Example applications: discovering loaded dice, detecting small diurnal barometer variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of residual phenomena by averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: If after many trials the average result is non-zero and stable (instead of cancelling to zero), that residual indicates the presence and magnitude of some small constant cause previously obscured by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use averaging across diverse circumstances to reveal small systematic effects (residuals). Authors should report how the mean changes with additional trials and justify sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of sample size and expected variation (theory of chances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond long-run averages, one must consider what deviations from expected chance levels are credible in finite samples; this requires the doctrine of chances (Theory of Probabilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply probabilistic reasoning to assess whether observed deviations in limited samples could plausibly arise by chance. Peer reviewers should expect appropriate probability-based calculations when sample sizes are small or when assessing extreme deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation of probability calculations — equally possible cases or empirical frequencies
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply Laplacean probability methods, one must identify equally possible cases (states about which we are equally undecided), but empirical confirmation (observed equal frequencies) may be necessary in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that assumptions of equiprobability are justified (either analytically or empirically). If equiprobability is unjustified, probability estimates may be invalid.
